reference.source: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry / Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
clinicalPearls: Urea cycle converts toxic ammonia to urea; initial 2 steps are mitochondrial (CPS-I, OTC); final 3 steps are cytosolic (ASS, ASL, arginase)
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I (CPS-I) is rate-limiting and requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligate allosteric activator
Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is X-linked recessive; carbamoyl phosphate spills into cytosol, causing massive urinary orotic acid
Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) features normal blood ammonia, whereas OTC deficiency features severe hyperammonemia
Ammonia neurotoxicity: drives glutamate dehydrogenase toward glutamate, depleting alpha-ketoglutarate; astrocyte glutamine accumulation causes brain edema
reference.pathophysiology: Urea cycle enzyme defects prevent nitrogen disposal, causing acute hyperammonemic encephalopathy in neonates shortly after protein feeds begin. Excess ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier, where astrocytes convert it to glutamine via glutamine synthetase. Intracellular glutamine functions as an osmolyte, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension.
additionalInvestigations: Plasma ammonia (normal <35 mcmol/L; >150 mcmol/L in neonate is medical emergency)
Plasma amino acid analysis (citrulline, arginine, glutamine)
Urine organic acid and orotic acid quantitation
